messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sofia's eyes would often glaze over, her mind transported back to that fateful night eight years ago when she and her partner were held captive by a group of assailants while responding to an emergency call. The memory was etched in her brain like a scar – the sound of shattering glass, the feeling of being dragged away from the safety of their ambulance, the smell of sweat and fear that clung to her skin long after they were finally freed. Even now, as a seasoned paramedic with over three decades of experience, Sofia couldn't shake off the sense of helplessness that crept in whenever she thought about that night. "I was so powerless," she would whisper to herself, "I couldn't even protect myself." As she delved deeper into her memories, the emotions came flooding back – a tidal wave of feelings that left her breathless and disoriented. It was as if the experience had become a living, breathing entity that threatened to consume her at any moment. When the memories resurfaced, Sofia felt like she was drowning in an ocean of fear, unable to keep her head above water. Her mind would start racing, her thoughts careening wildly from one catastrophic scenario to another – what if they came back? What if she wasn't prepared? The more she tried to push the memories away, the more they seemed to force their way into her consciousness, unbidden and unwelcome. Sofia had come to believe that her reactions since the event were a sign of her own fragility – proof that she was indeed going crazy. She felt like she was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the memories would strike again or what new horrors they might bring with them. Her world had shrunk to a tiny, suffocating space where every silence seemed menacing and every shadow hid a potential threat. Even in her own home – that supposed sanctuary – Sofia felt like she was constantly on guard, waiting for the other shoe to drop. As she navigated the familiar streets of her neighborhood, Sofia found herself frequently checking behind her, half-expecting to see someone lurking in the shadows. Her friends and family had grown accustomed to her nervous habits – the constant looking over her shoulder, the way she would freeze at sudden noises – but they couldn't understand why these behaviors persisted long after the trauma should have faded into memory. Sofia herself didn't know; all she knew was that the memories had become a constant companion, one that whispered dark fears in her ear and refused to let her go. Despite her best efforts to keep them at bay, the memories continued to haunt Sofia – an unwelcome presence that seeped into every corner of her life. It was as if they had developed a twisted symbiosis, feeding off each other's darkness until the threat felt omnipresent and suffocating. And yet, it was this very cycle that kept Sofia trapped in a prison of her own making – afraid to confront the memories head-on, too scared to let go of the fears that bound her. As she sat in her living room now, surrounded by the familiar comforts of home, Sofia felt like she was staring into an abyss. The memories loomed large, casting long shadows across her mind and heart. She knew she couldn't keep running from them – not anymore. With a deep breath, she reached for the phone and dialed the number of a therapist, hoping against hope that someone might finally be able to help her break free from this prison of fear and silence.
